texts.t49_J1h1:
# Sometimes There Isn't a Clear Child Yet

Reparenting assumes there's a clear little one in there to love, and for a lot of people there is. But if you grew up somewhere you only belonged as long as you played somebody else, like a really controlling family or a strict church, the real one may never have had room to form. All this stuff about your little one could have left you wondering who I'm even talking about.

Maybe you started playing that part so early, and it took over so completely, that "What do I believe?" or "What do I want?" has no clear answer of your own. They sound like such easy questions, too. Back then, asking might have gotten you in trouble, or laughed at. Or there was just no way to ask. That can make "love yourself" feel pretty empty (love what, when the part you've been playing doesn't feel real?).

## From Survival to Experimental Play

If your childhood meant avoiding pain and keeping the people you needed close, your attention got used up reading danger (was that sigh about me?) and meeting their expectations, and when curiosity or mistakes got you punished, or it felt like they loved you less, you got better at the part. That left much less room for experiments that show you what you like when nobody's grading you. People grow into who they are by trying things on and then changing their minds, from what they wear down to the ideas and roles they take up, like a teenager who starts spelling her name with an "i" at the end and later changes it back.

Some of this is developmental pl/ork you get to do late: making it safe enough for your curiosity and experimenting to finally grow, and your preferences too. It might feel wrong somehow to like something before you've checked anyone's face. You can usually reparent and build who you are at the same time, but if your little one isn't easy to feel yet, making it safe like that is the first phase.

As you tell the part you've been playing apart from the self that didn't get much practice, notice whether it makes you more curious about both, and better able to relate to them. Or does it have you thinking, "That one's fake, and I'm getting rid of it"? You're after a relationship between them inside you that works better, and that's hard to have if there's a new split between an acceptable self and one that has to disappear.

That's assuming the self that didn't get much practice is easy to find, though. Your preferences and beliefs might shift a lot with the people around you, and you might not know what you'd choose without the fear of disappointing somebody. And when you ask what your little one feels, maybe all you get is a guess (which isn't proof there's no little one in there), something like "lonely, probably?"

So early on, the practice is finding out who's actually in there, through long reflection with no outside input, and journaling just for yourself, without picturing a reader. You might catch yourself explaining who everybody is anyway. Time alone in nature helps too, and so does getting back the preferences that got buried: the foods you really like and what feels good to do, and what you believe and feel when nobody's around to take your cues from.

Focusing (Eugene Gendlin's method of listening to a vague, felt sense in your body) can especially help you notice feelings and preferences the part you've been playing learned to overlook. Any words you put to them can stay tentative ("I hate cooking... or just for everybody?") while you look at what they seem to mean and revise how you read them. Some people also benefit from temporary, intentional distance from whoever they've been playing the part for, long enough for conditioning to quiet down and real preferences to surface.

## Untangling the Belonging Bargains

Part of building who you are is untangling yourself from whatever pulls you away from your own knowing in return for belonging, like a political tribe or another group you identify with which expects consistent positions and predictable reactions. Or the expectations of a family or religion that’s kind to you. Going along with those might just feel like being good. Most groups expect some conformity, which is ordinary, like your family wanting a particular kind of son or daughter, or your friends’ rules about what you can joke about or get upset about. But if going along means betraying yourself, that’s the bargain.
texts.t49_P2: Then there's another bargain, where you have to earn your worth: when you don't feel your value inside, you can become a "human doer," working for it in some arena outside yourself. That might be beauty, athleticism or sexual desirability, or intelligence and grades. For some people it's money or status, and for others it's a sophisticated spiritual identity or becoming indispensable to everybody else's problems. It can feel really good to be the one everybody calls. In its controlling form, that caretaking can drift into keeping other people dependent, because being needed has become the caretaker's main source of value.
texts.t49_P3: Beauty, intelligence, achievement and caretaking can all be real gifts, but they become belonging bargains when failing in the arena feels like losing yourself. Your little one, with nobody parenting it, takes those bargains to survive, because belonging feels like life or death. That happens to children of good parents too, and it isn't a flaw in you. Noticing where you're betraying yourself to belong, and keeping your own ground, is called self-differentiation. It also means noticing when praise or pity suddenly changes what you think you know, or fear or attraction does, or something that really resonates with you.
texts.t49_H1: Pema Chödrön has a quick map for finding the bargain. It's four pairs, starting with pleasure and pain, and gain and loss. The other two are about what people think of you: praise and blame, and good reputation and disgrace. Your little one can panic when something hurts, and also when something good might disappear, like praise, romance, money, status, belonging or a spiritual high. You might still be enjoying one of those when your little one starts asking how long this is going to last.
texts.t49_H3: The aim isn't to stop enjoying pleasure or praise, though, and the same goes for gain and belonging. It's noticing when one of them has turned into a condition for having a self. Maybe some part of you is sure that if you lost it, there wouldn't be much of you left.
texts.t49_H4: Differentiation can happen right inside a family or a religion, and the same goes for a community or a relationship. You'd be belonging selectively, which still leaves room to belong. As a differentiated adult you can stay deeply embedded, free to question things or disagree, and if staying would mean disappearing, you're free to leave. If a parent used to go quiet and hurt whenever you disagreed, that might be hard to believe. A family where everyone gets to be their own person is healthier than an enmeshed one, and a faith that's your own is healthier than religious compliance. It can be the same religion either way. And two differentiated people have a sturdier relationship than two who've been absorbed into each other.
texts.t49_H2:
When that happens, you can ask yourself these, once you've caught your breath:
- What do I think I'm about to gain or lose?
- Whose approval suddenly feels like survival? It isn't always who you'd guess.
- Am I protecting a real value, or trying to preserve a high?
- What would still be worth doing if nobody praised me for it?

texts.t49_H5:
Day to day, differentiation looks something like this:
- Other people's emotions and opinions stop automatically replacing your own. Their reasons can still change your mind, though.
- Noticing when you agreed in the moment and disagree later: "Wait, why was I nodding along?"
- Caring about somebody's feelings without sacrificing your own ground.
- Disappointing people and withstanding social pressure, and still being recognizably yourself wherever you are (maybe louder in some places). That one can take a while.
- Questioning what you were programmed to believe while holding the discomfort, and without having to stop loving anyone over it.
texts.t49_H2d:
When that happens, you can ask yourself these, once you've caught your breath:
- What do I think I'm about to get, or lose?
- Whose approval suddenly feels like I can't live without it? It isn't always who you'd guess.
- Is this a value I'm standing up for, or a high I'm trying to keep?
- Would this still be worth doing if nobody praised me for it?
texts.t49_H2e: When that happens, once you've caught your breath, it can help to ask what you think you're about to gain or lose, and whose approval suddenly feels like survival. It isn't always who you'd guess. Is it a real value you're protecting, or a high you're trying to keep? And what would still be worth doing if nobody praised you for it?
texts.t49_H6: Differentiation is slow, and it goes on your whole life. If a family, group or relationship won't let you do this while you're still part of it, temporary distance may be necessary. Some people come back later on different terms. Sometimes the leaving turns out to be permanent, because going back would mean disappearing again. You don't have to know yet which one yours is. As you differentiate, you learn to tell the difference.
